phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bridge'; Old Norse initial b is fully voiced.
Trilled [r] followed by the close front rounded vowel [y] — the sound of German 'ü' or French 'tu'; the first element bryn-, 'mail-coat', stressed as the head of the compound.
Voiceless glottal [h], short [i], lateral [l], voiced stop [d], and the syllabic trill [r̩] of the nominative ending — the second element hildr, 'battle', one of the commonest name-words in Germanic.

pronunciation.approximation: BRÜN-hild-r — the y is the rounded front vowel of German 'ü'; stress the first syllable; the final -r is the nominative ending, lightly sounded, as in modern Icelandic Brynhildur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Brynhildr, the valkyrie of the Vǫlsung cycle; also Sigrdrífa, 'victory-urger', the name Sigrdrífumál itself gives her.

kin.label: Old High German
kin.form: Brünhilt, the haughty queen of the Nibelungenlied and Þiðreks saga.

kin.label: Wagnerian
kin.form: Brünnhilde, the Valkyrie of the Ring cycle, built from the Norse rather than the German sources.

kin.label: Historical
kin.form: Brunhilda, the Merovingian queen of Austrasia (d. 613), long linked by scholars to the legendary name.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Brynhildur, the name's unbroken living form.

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Brynhildr is a transparent compound: bryn- 'mail-coat, byrnie' (the noun brynja) + hildr 'battle' — 'armor battle', the battle-maid in her mail. The normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII: no diacritic, no thorn, no eth for the restoration to recover. Tier-2 by the mechanical rule: nothing distinctive is lost in transit — a statement about orthography, never about the figure.

domains.title: Valkyrie, Shieldmaiden
domains.subtitle: The Sleep-Thorn, the Wall of Flame, and the Pyre of the Dragonslayer
domains.lead: Brynhildr is the valkyrie of the Vǫlsung cycle: the battle-maid Óðinn pricked with the sleep-thorn for defying his judgment, the shieldmaiden Sigurðr woke behind a wall of flame, the sworn beloved whom a draught of forgetfulness and a changed shape betrayed — and the woman who would not outlive the deceit, burning herself on the dragonslayer's pyre with a drawn sword between them.

cards.name: The Sleep-Thorn
cards.desc: Svefnþorn — the thorn Óðinn struck her with for giving victory against his word: sleep as sentence, and the beginning of the whole tragedy.

cards.name: The Vafrlogi
cards.desc: The flickering wall of flame around her hall on Hindarfjall — crossable only by Grani, only by Sigurðr, and later only by a borrowed shape.

cards.name: The Drawn Sword
cards.desc: Gramr laid naked between the lovers three nights — and laid between them again on the pyre, the sign of the bed that was never shared.

cards.name: Andvaranautr
cards.desc: The ring from the dwarf's hoard, taken in the exchanged shapes and produced at the quarrel — the small gold proof that undid a kingdom.

symbols.name: The sleep-thorn (svefnþorn)
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's sentence on disobedience — sleep as the price of an independent judgment

symbols.name: The wall of flame (vafrlogi)
symbols.meaning: The test that admits only the fearless — the fire no coward's horse will cross

symbols.name: The byrnie grown fast to her flesh
symbols.meaning: War-gear become skin: the valkyrie so long asleep that armor and woman had to be cut apart

symbols.name: The drawn sword between the lovers
symbols.meaning: The chaste bed of the deception — and the same sword laid between them in death

symbols.name: The ring Andvaranautr
symbols.meaning: The token that proves what memory was made to forget — gold as witness

mythology.lead: Brynhildr's story is the tragic core of the Vǫlsung cycle — told across Sigrdrífumál, the Guðrún poems, Sigurðarkviða hin skamma, Helreið Brynhildar, and Vǫlsunga saga with a consistency the corpus rarely achieves: the sentence, the waking, the oath, the deceit, the quarrel, the pyre.

myths.title: The Valkyrie's Sentence
myths.text: The prose frame of Sigrdrífumál gives her the name Sigrdrífa, 'victory-urger', and tells how she fell: two kings fought, Hjálmgunnarr the old and Agnar the young, and Óðinn had promised the victory to Hjálmgunnarr. The valkyrie judged otherwise and gave the day to Agnar. Óðinn pricked her with the sleep-thorn in revenge and declared she should never again fight in victory and should be given in marriage — and she answered that she had bound herself with an oath to wed no man who knew fear. The whole tragedy is already here: a woman whose only crime was an independent verdict, sentenced to sleep until a fearless man should come.

myths.title: The Waking on Hindarfjall
myths.text: Sigurðr, fresh from Fáfnir's hoard, saw a light on Hindarfjall as though a fire burned to the sky, and rode Grani through the vafrlogi — the horse would take no other rider through that flame. Within the wall stood a hall, and in the hall a figure in full armor. He cut the byrnie from her with Gramr, from the neck down, for it had grown fast to her flesh, and she woke and asked what had strength to break her sleep. 'Sigmundr's son,' he answered, 'with the sword that has lately slain Fáfnir.' She taught him then the runes of victory and the counsels of Sigrdrífumál — how to carve, how to trust, how to beware — and they plighted their troth, the valkyrie and the dragonslayer, before fate had its word.

myths.title: The Ale of Forgetfulness
myths.text: At the court of Gjúki, Queen Grímhildr gave Sigurðr a draught of forgetfulness, and the memory of Brynhildr went out of him like a light; he married Guðrún and swore brotherhood with Gunnarr and Hǫgni. Then Gunnarr desired Brynhildr — but his horse would not take the flame. By Grímhildr's craft the two men exchanged shapes: Sigurðr rode the vafrlogi in Gunnarr's form, won the bride for his sworn brother, and lay three nights beside her with the drawn sword Gramr between them. Before they parted he took from her hand the ring Andvaranautr and gave her another ring from Fáfnir's hoard. Every element of the catastrophe is a theft so small it could hide in a draught, a shape, a ring.

myths.title: The Quarrel of the Queens
myths.text: It broke at the river. Brynhildr and Guðrún went to the water to wash their hair, and Brynhildr waded the farther out, for her husband had ridden the flame, and Gunnarr's was the greater deed. Guðrún answered with the truth: it was Sigurðr who rode through in Gunnarr's shape — and she held up Andvaranautr, the ring taken from Brynhildr's own hand that night, as proof. Brynhildr knew the ring and turned white as a dead woman, and went home and spoke no word that evening. The German Nibelungenlied keeps the same wound in a different key: the queens' quarrel at the minster door, and Brünhilt learning that it was Siegfried who mastered her for Gunther. In both traditions the betrayal is revealed by a woman to a woman, and the world comes down after.

myths.title: The Pyre and the Road to Hel
myths.text: Brynhildr could not live inside the deceit, and she would not let it stand: she turned Gunnarr to vengeance, and Sigurðr was slain in his bed by young Guthormr, the one brother bound by no oath — the dying hero cast Gramr after his killer and cut him in two. When Guðrún's wail rose over the body, Brynhildr laughed once, from the bottom of her heart; then she took a sword and stabbed herself, and with her death upon her gave her last commands: to be burned on the pyre beside Sigurðr, with a drawn sword between them as it had been before, 'when we both entered one bed and were called by the name of man and wife.' Helreið Brynhildar follows her past the fire: on the road to Hel a giantess by her mound chides her for the blood on her hands, and Brynhildr answers with her whole life — the sleep, the waking, the oath kept, the deceit endured. 'Let us ride together,' the poem has her say, toward the place where Sigurðr waits.

lore.syncretism: Brynhildr lives two lives in the medieval record. The Norse tradition — Sigrdrífumál, the heroic lays, Vǫlsunga saga — makes her a valkyrie, sentenced by Óðinn and woken by Sigurðr. The continental tradition makes her human: the Nibelungenlied's Brünhilt is the proud queen of Iceland whose strength no suitor could master until Siegfried, invisible in his cloak of power, won her for Gunther; Þiðreks saga stands between the two, keeping a martial Brunhild in the far north. Since the Grimms, scholars have linked the legendary name to the historical Brunhilda of Austrasia, the Merovingian queen executed in 613 — a connection plausible for the continental strand and unnecessary for the Norse. Wagner refused the choice: his Brünnhilde is built from the Norse sources, Wotan's daughter and Siegfried's doom, and the Grimm brothers had already heard the svefnþorn echoing in the thorn-hedged sleep of Dornröschen — the fairy tale keeping the valkyrie's sentence alive in the nursery.
lore.culturalLegacy: Brynhildr's modern afterlife is Wagner's: the Ring cycle made Brünnhilde the most famous valkyrie in the world, and her immolation — riding Grane into Siegfried's pyre with the ring returned to the Rhine — is opera's great closing image of a world redeemed by a woman's refusal to accept its lies. Behind Wagner stand the Victorian rediscoveries: Morris's Sigurd the Volsung gave English readers the whole arc, sleep-thorn to pyre. The archetype she fixed — the warrior woman asleep behind fire, won only by the fearless — runs through the fairy tale of Sleeping Beauty and every later shieldmaiden of fiction. In Iceland the name never left: Brynhildur remains a living given name, and Old Norse Brynhildr stays the standard citation form in every handbook of heroic legend.
lore.extendedMeditation: Brynhildr is the tradition's figure of the oath that outlives its world. Everything taken from her is taken by small magic — a thorn, a draught, a borrowed shape, a ring — and none of it touches the thing she actually is: the woman who judged rightly against a god, who asked only for a man without fear, and who kept her account with the truth to the last breath. Her one laugh, heard as the world breaks, is among the most unsettling sounds in the Edda; her pyre, with the drawn sword between the dead, is its clearest statement that a marriage made by deceit could be annulled only by fire. The cycle does not ask us to forgive her vengeance. It asks whether any of the men around her — the forgetful hero, the oath-bound brothers, the scheming queen — ever matched the standard she set: to know what happened, and to refuse to pretend otherwise.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Brynhildr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᚱᚢᚾᚼᛁᛚᛏᚱ (b-r-u-n-h-i-l-t-R, the ᚢ rune covering u and y alike, and the ᛏ rune writing both t and d). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: brynhildr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Brynhildr herself has no cult site, votive deposit, or named image — she is a figure of heroic legend, not of cult. The material record attests the legend around her. The Sigurðr carvings of Södermanland — the Ramsund carving (Sö 101) and the Gök stone (Sö 327), both eleventh century — depict the slaying of Fáfnir, the roasting heart, the talking birds, and the slain Reginn, proving the Vǫlsung cycle's visual currency in the late Viking Age. The carved portal of Hylestad stave church in Norway (c. 1200) retells the saga's scenes in wood, and the Kirk Andreas cross on the Isle of Man shows Sigurðr roasting the dragon's heart. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows a woman offering a drinking horn to a rider, sometimes interpreted as Sigrdrífa or Brynhildr, though the identification is debated. The textual witnesses hang on thin threads: the heroic lays survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) — with the famous lacuna of a lost gathering that Brot af Sigurðarkviðu breaks across — and Vǫlsunga saga is preserved in a vellum fragment (NGU 182 4to) and paper copies.
